pos: n. (the kingdom reformed by Christian III at the Diet of Copenhagen in 1536, whose Bible of 1550 served three northern nations)
etymology: Danish Danmark, the march of the Danes; Latin Dania.
biblical_def: Denmark is the northern kingdom where the Reformation was carried by preaching and completed by a coup. Lutheran books came through the Hanseatic ports in the early 1520s; Hans Tausen, a Danish monk who had studied at Wittenberg, began preaching evangelically at Viborg in 1526 and became the movement's chief Danish voice, publishing a Danish hymnal, a postil and a translation of the Pentateuch. Malmo and the Jutland towns reformed under their own councils through the 1520s and 1530s while the crown was disputed. The settlement came with the Count's War: Christian III, already a Lutheran from his years in Holstein, won the kingdom, arrested the bishops in August 1536, and had the Diet of Copenhagen abolish the episcopate, confiscate the church lands to the crown, and establish the Reformation; Johannes Bugenhagen came from Wittenberg to write the church ordinance of 1537, crown the king, and ordain the seven new superintendents. Peder Palladius, superintendent of Zealand, then spent twenty years visiting every parish in his diocese and left a visitation book that is the best picture of a reformed countryside in Europe. Christian III's Danish Bible appeared in 1550. The dictionary enters Denmark because its reformation was legally the most abrupt in Europe and pastorally among the most thorough.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an episcopate as the office of a bishop; to confiscate as to adjudge property forfeit to the public; a visitation as the act of visiting for inspection; and a postil as a short exposition of the gospel.
webster_full: EPISCOPATE, n. A bishopric; the office and dignity of a bishop; the order of bishops.
CONFISCATE, v. To adjudge to be forfeited to the public treasury, as the goods of a criminal.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting for the purpose of inspection, or the examination of a church or diocese.
POSTIL, n. A marginal note; a short exposition or homily upon the gospel of the day.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
scriptures: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Eze 34:4

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
corruption_summary: Northern kingdom reformed at the Diet of Copenhagen in 1536, ordered by Bugenhagen's ordinance of 1537, and given a Danish Bible in 1550.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the confiscation that enriches a crown and starves a parish. The Danish church lands went to Christian III, and although the ordinance of 1537 provided stipends, schools and poor relief out of them, the crown took the larger share and the rural clergy were poor for centuries. The prophet's indictment of the shepherds of Israel is the measure: “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4), and a reformation that reorganises revenues without feeding the flock has repeated the fault it came to correct.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the visitation, which Palladius turned into the best feature of the Danish settlement: a superintendent going parish by parish, examining the minister, catechising the people, and writing down what he found. “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2) is the office he exercised, and the apostolic pattern he followed was to teach “publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20). The promise over such an arrangement is that “I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15).

pos: n. (the kingdom where Gustav Vasa took the church's wealth in 1527 and the Reformation of doctrine followed slowly behind)
etymology: Swedish Sverige, the realm of the Svear; Latin Suecia.
biblical_def: Sweden is the kingdom in which the Reformation was begun by a king who wanted the church's money and finished by churchmen who wanted its doctrine, and the sixty-six years between the two are the point. Gustav Vasa, having won independence from Denmark in 1523, needed revenue, and at the Diet of Vasteras in 1527 he obtained the transfer of church property to the crown and the subordination of the bishops to himself; he was not much interested in the theological questions. Olaus Petri, a Wittenberg student, carried those: he published the Swedish New Testament in 1526, a Swedish mass in 1531, a manual, a postil and a hymnal, and shaped the liturgy that the Church of Sweden has kept. His brother Laurentius Petri became the first evangelical archbishop of Uppsala in 1531, held the office for forty-two years, completed the Gustav Vasa Bible in 1541, and wrote the church ordinance of 1571; and because he outlasted three kings he was able to keep the episcopate, the liturgy and the apostolic succession of orders that make Sweden's Reformation unlike any other Lutheran settlement. The Uppsala Assembly of 1593 finally bound the kingdom to the Augsburg Confession. The dictionary enters Sweden because the slow way proved durable, and because the king's motive was plainly avarice and God used it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines avarice as an inordinate desire of gain; succession as a following in order; a liturgy as a formulary of public prayers; and an archbishop as the chief of the bishops of a province.
webster_full: AVARICE, n. An inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness of gain.
SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; the act of succeeding or coming in the place of another.
LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public prayers.
ARCHBISHOP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class; a metropolitan bishop.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite.
scriptures: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Kingdom whose Diet of Vasteras in 1527 transferred church property to Gustav Vasa, while Olaus and Laurentius Petri carried the Reformation of doctrine and liturgy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reform undertaken for money, and the dictionary says plainly that this is what Vasteras was. Gustav Vasa needed to pay his debts to Lubeck, the church held a fifth of the land, and the diet gave it to him; his later quarrels with the Petri brothers were about his authority and his revenue, not about justification. The apostolic warning is the right text over the transaction: “the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10). That the Swedish church nonetheless received a vernacular Bible, a sound liturgy and a catechising ministry out of those years is the pattern of Joseph's word to his brothers: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a slow reformation held by patient churchmen outlasts a swift one imposed by a prince. Laurentius Petri held the see of Uppsala for forty-two years and used them to translate, to write an ordinance and to outlive the kings who interfered, and “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9) is as true of an archbishop as of a monarch. The fruit was that Swedes heard “in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) from 1526.

pos: n. (the kingdom on which the Reformation was imposed from Denmark in 1537, and which got its own revival from a farmer in 1796)
etymology: Norwegian Norge, from Old Norse Norðrvegr, the north way, the sea route along the coast.
biblical_def: Norway is the northern kingdom that received the Reformation as an act of a foreign crown and did not receive its own religious awakening for two hundred and sixty years. Christian III, having won Denmark in 1536, declared Norway a Danish province in 1537 and extended Bugenhagen's ordinance to it; the archbishop of Nidaros fled with the cathedral treasury, the monasteries were dissolved, and Danish-speaking clergy were appointed over a Norwegian-speaking people. Danish became the language of the church, the Bible and the school, and remained so; Norwegian had no Bible of its own until the nineteenth century. Geble Pedersson, the first evangelical bishop of Bergen, and later Erik Pontoppidan with his catechism explanation of 1737, did real work inside that framework. The change came from outside the clergy altogether. Hans Nielsen Hauge, a farmer's son of Tune, began in 1796 to travel the country on foot preaching repentance and faith, wrote tracts that sold in tens of thousands, gathered lay assemblies, and was repeatedly imprisoned under the Conventicle Ordinance of 1741, which forbade religious meetings not led by a parish minister. The dictionary enters Norway because its Reformation was imposed and its revival was prosecuted, and both facts are about the same arrangement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as a private assembly for worship; a tract as a short treatise; an awakening as a revival of religion; and an ordinance as a rule established by authority.
webster_full: CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; a secret or private assembly for religious worship, applied reproachfully.
TRACT, n. A written discourse or dissertation of less extent than a book; a short treatise.
AWAKENING, n. A revival of religion, or more general attention to spiritual concerns than usual.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
LAYMAN, n. A man not a clergyman; one of the laity or people distinct from the clergy.
scriptures: Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: Kingdom made a Danish province in 1537 and reformed by foreign ordinance, where Hans Nielsen Hauge's lay preaching from 1796 was prosecuted under the Conventicle Ordinance.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the law that makes the preaching of the gospel a licensed trade. The Conventicle Ordinance of 1741 forbade a Norwegian to gather his neighbours for prayer and Scripture unless the parish minister led it, and Hauge was jailed again and again under it, spending years in prison and his health with them. The apostles answered the same prohibition in the same way: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). What followed Hauge's preaching was what follows such preaching, that “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God calls men out of ordinary trades to speak for him and is not bound by an establishment's roll. Amos answered a priest who told him to go home with “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman” (Amo 7:14). Hauge was a farmer who could write, and the apostolic account of such choices is that “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1Co 1:27). Norway's established church afterwards absorbed much of what he began.

pos: n. (the North Atlantic island whose Reformation gave it a complete Bible in its own tongue in 1584, and whose last Catholic bishop was beheaded)
etymology: Icelandic Ísland, the land of ice, named by the Norse settlers of the ninth century; the tongue is the most conservative of the Scandinavian languages.
biblical_def: Iceland is the remote island where the Reformation arrived by royal decree and produced, almost at once, one of the best vernacular Bibles in Europe. Danish officials brought the ordinance of 1537 and met resistance; Jon Arason, bishop of Holar and the last Catholic bishop in Iceland, held the north against it, raised men, and was taken and beheaded with his two sons at Skalholt in November 1550 without trial, an act the dictionary names as judicial murder whatever his doctrine. What the Reformation did well in Iceland was translate. Oddur Gottskalksson, a bishop's son who had learned Lutheran doctrine abroad, translated the New Testament into Icelandic in a cowshed at Skalholt, as the story goes, and it was printed at Roskilde in 1540, the first book ever printed in Icelandic. Gudbrandur Thorlaksson, bishop of Holar for over fifty years from 1571, set up a press at Holar, revised and completed the whole Bible, and printed it there in 1584 in five hundred copies, enough for every church in the country, a book so good that its language is still a standard. The dictionary enters Iceland because a population of perhaps fifty thousand on a volcanic island got a whole printed Bible in their own speech before most of Europe did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; a cowshed as a shelter for cattle; beheading as the act of severing the head; and an edition as the whole number of copies published at once.
webster_full: PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.
SHED, n. A slight or temporary building; a penthouse or hovel; a covering for shelter.
BEHEAD, v. To cut off the head; to sever the head from the body with a cutting instrument.
EDITION, n. The publication of any book; the whole number of copies of a work published at once.
ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded with water; a piece of land not connected with a continent.

Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
Isa 51:5
My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust.
Isa 49:1
Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The LORD hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name.
corruption_summary: North Atlantic island reformed by royal ordinance in 1537, whose last Catholic bishop was beheaded in 1550 and whose complete Icelandic Bible was printed at Holar in 1584.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the execution without trial of a defeated opponent, which is what happened to Jon Arason and his sons at Skalholt in 1550. He had taken up arms against the royal officers, and the dictionary neither approves his doctrine nor his rising; it holds that a man captured in such a quarrel is owed a hearing and a sentence, and that the Danish officials who had him beheaded on their own authority committed murder. The rule of the kingdom is not changed by the convenience of the executioner, and the isles that wait for the Lord's law “shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4) also wait for his justice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the promise made to the islands and the far places, which Iceland fulfils as exactly as any country in Europe. “Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far” (Isa 49:1) is addressed to men at the edge of the known world, and the response is the psalm's, “let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1). Five hundred Bibles printed at Holar in 1584, one for every church on the island, is what “the isles shall wait upon me” (Isa 51:5) came to mean in Icelandic.

pos: n. (the Danish peninsula whose town of Viborg heard Hans Tausen from 1526, where the Danish Reformation began)
etymology: Danish Jylland, the land of the Jutes; the peninsula running north from Holstein between the North Sea and the Kattegat.
biblical_def: Jutland is the Danish peninsula where evangelical preaching began before any king had decided anything. Hans Tausen, a Danish Hospitaller monk who had studied at Wittenberg and come home with Luther's doctrine, was placed in the order's house at Viborg and from 1526 preached there; the townsmen protected him, the burghers took the Grey Friars' church for him, and Viborg became the first reformed town in the kingdom. Frederick I made him his chaplain in 1526, which was as far as a king who had sworn to defend the old church could prudently go. Aalborg, Aarhus, Ribe and Randers followed, each by its own council and preacher, and the Jutland nobility was divided; when the Count's War came the peninsula was fought over hard, and the peasant risings of 1534 in northern Jutland were put down with great slaughter at Aalborg. Jorgen Sadolin, Tausen's brother-in-law, ran a school for evangelical preachers at Viborg and later became superintendent of Funen. The dictionary enters Jutland because the Danish Reformation is usually dated from the diet of 1536 and actually began ten years earlier in a provincial market town, carried by burghers who wanted a preacher and kept him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friar as a brother of a religious order; a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough; a chaplain as a clergyman attached to a court; and a peninsula as land almost surrounded by water.
webster_full: FRIAR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town; one who possesses a municipal right.
CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the charge of a chapel; a clergyman attached to a court, an army or a family.
PENINSULA, n. A portion of land almost surrounded by water, joined to the mainland by a neck or isthmus.
PULPIT, n. An elevated place or enclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands.

And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.

For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe.
Act 17:4
And some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas; and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few.
corruption_summary: Danish peninsula where Hans Tausen preached at Viborg from 1526, making it the kingdom's first reformed town ten years before the diet of 1536.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the dating of a reformation from its legislation, which flatters princes and hides congregations. Viborg's burghers heard a preacher, judged his doctrine, took a church for him and defended him against his own order, and they did it a decade before the crown settled anything. What they did is the thing Scripture records of the Thessalonians, who received the preaching “not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God” (1Th 2:13), and that reception is the reformation, whatever the statute book says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church is formed by a people continuing in the apostles' doctrine, and the first Christian congregations are described in exactly those terms: they “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42). Jutland's towns did that one at a time, as the men of Thessalonica did when “some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas” (Act 17:4). The naming follows the believing, for “the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch” (Act 11:26) and not by a diet.

pos: n. (the southern province, Danish Skåne, where Malmo reformed first and the first Danish liturgy was printed in 1529)
etymology: Latin Scania, Danish and Swedish Skåne, of disputed Germanic root; Danish until 1658 and Swedish since.
biblical_def: Scania is the province, Danish for seven centuries and Swedish since 1658, whose chief town carried the Danish Reformation before the kingdom did. Malmo, a prosperous herring and trading port facing Copenhagen across the sound, took evangelical preaching from 1527 under Claus Mortensen and Hans Olufsen Spandemager; the town council backed them, the Grey Friars' church was given over, and in 1529 Malmo printed the first Danish evangelical service book and hymnal, the Malmo Mass, which put the liturgy, the Lord's Prayer and the congregational hymns into Danish for the first time and became the basis of the Danish rite. Frands Vormordsen, a Dutch Carmelite turned Lutheran who taught Hebrew, worked there on the Psalms and became the first evangelical superintendent of Lund. Lund itself, the ancient archbishopric of the whole north, lost its primacy at the Reformation and became a Lutheran see, and its university came only in 1666 after the Swedish conquest. The dictionary enters Scania because the first Danish liturgy and hymnal were produced by a town council and two preachers in a herring port, seven years before the kingdom was reformed by law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a formulary of public prayers; a hymnal as a collection of hymns; a see as the seat of a bishop; and a primacy as the chief ecclesiastical dignity.
webster_full: LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public prayers.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a sacred lyric sung in public worship.
SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
PRIMACY, n. The chief ecclesiastical station or dignity; the office or dignity of an archbishop.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
scriptures: Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
corruption_summary: Southern province, Danish until 1658, where Malmo reformed from 1527 and printed the first Danish evangelical service book and hymnal in 1529.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the congregation reduced to an audience, which a Latin liturgy enforces whether anyone intends it or not. In the old rite the people could not say the responses, could not pray the prayers and did not sing; the Malmo book of 1529 handed them all three in Danish. The apostle's objection to prayer in an unknown tongue is exactly this: “how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?” (1Co 14:16).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is congregational singing as a means of teaching, which the Reformation's hymnals were built for. The command is to teach one another, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16), and the manner is given as “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). A trading town with a press obeyed the psalm's charge to “Sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 149:1) by printing one that herring-fishers could read.

pos: n. (the eastern half of the Swedish realm, where Mikael Agricola made Finnish a written language for the sake of the gospel)
etymology: Swedish Finland, the land of the Finns; Finnish Suomi. The tongue is Finnic and unrelated to Swedish.
biblical_def: Finland is the country whose written language was created by one man in order to preach to it. It was the eastern half of the kingdom of Sweden, governed in Swedish, with a Finnish-speaking peasantry who had almost nothing in their own tongue; Finnish had never been a printed language. Mikael Agricola, a shoemaker's son of Pernaja, studied at Wittenberg under Luther and Melanchthon, returned to Turku in 1539 as rector of its cathedral school and later its bishop, and set himself to supply a Finnish church with Finnish books. He published about 1543 the Abckiria, a primer and catechism, the first book ever printed in Finnish; a prayer book of nearly nine hundred pages in 1544; and in 1548 the New Testament in Finnish, with portions of the Old Testament following. He had to invent orthography, coin vocabulary for doctrine the language had no words for, and pay for much of the printing himself; he died in 1557 at forty-seven, worn out, returning from an embassy to Russia. Paul Juusten carried the work on. The dictionary enters Finland because the Reformation gave a whole nation its literature as a by-product of insisting that a peasant hear the gospel in the only language he had.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primer as an elementary book for instruction; orthography as the art of writing words with proper letters; a rector as the master of a school; and a vocabulary as a list of words.
webster_full: PRIMER, n. A small elementary book for religious instruction, or for teaching children to read.
ORTHOGRAPHY, n. The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage.
RECTOR, n. The master of a school; the head of a college; a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.
VOCABULARY, n. A list or collection of the words of a language, arranged in alphabetical order.
PRIMER, n. Also, a kind of type; but chiefly, the first book of instruction put into a child's hands.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
corruption_summary: Eastern half of the Swedish realm where Mikael Agricola created written Finnish, printing the first Finnish book about 1543 and the New Testament in 1548.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the judgement that a peasant language is not worth the labour of a scholar. Agricola had Wittenberg Latin, Greek and Hebrew and could have had a comfortable career in Swedish; he spent his life instead inventing a spelling, coining words for grace and justification that Finnish did not possess, and dying at forty-seven of overwork. The warrant is the apostle's preference: “I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also” (1Co 14:19).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the simple chain the apostle gives between the text and the hearer: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). A man who cannot hear it in a language he thinks in has not yet heard it. Pentecost is the standing answer to every argument of convenience, that each man heard “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) and spoke of hearing “them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11); and in 1548 that meant a Finnish New Testament printed at Stockholm at a bishop's own expense.

pos: n. (the Arctic island where the Norse church died out and Hans Egede began the Protestant mission to the Inuit in 1721)
etymology: Norse Grœnland, the green land, named by Erik the Red about 985 to attract settlers; Greenlandic Kalaallit Nunaat.
biblical_def: Greenland holds the one case in the north of a Christian church that simply disappeared, and the mission that went to look for it. Norse settlers had come about 985, built churches and a cathedral at Gardar, had a bishop, paid tithes to Rome, and then ceased: contact failed in the fifteenth century, the colonies died out, and when Europeans returned there were no Norsemen. Hans Egede, a Norwegian Lutheran pastor of Vagan, spent thirteen years petitioning Denmark to let him go and find them, sailed in 1721, found only Inuit, and turned to them instead. He stayed fifteen years, learned Kalaallisut, fought the whalers' brandy trade, buried his wife, and saw a smallpox epidemic in 1733 and 1734 kill a great part of the people he had come to; his son Paul Egede carried the work on and published the Greenlandic New Testament in 1766. The Moravians arrived in 1733 under Christian David and settled New Herrnhut beside him, and the two missions worked the same coast with some friction and much overlap. The dictionary enters Greenland because Egede went for one purpose, found it impossible, and did the harder thing he had not planned for, which is most of what missionary history actually consists of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending with commission to preach; a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country; brandy as a spirit distilled from wine; and a pestilence as a contagious disease.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending; persons sent with commission, as to preach the gospel in heathen lands.
COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province.
BRANDY, n. A spirit distilled from wine; a strong spirituous liquor.
PESTILENCE, n. Plague; pest; any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
CATECHUMEN, n. One who is receiving rudimentary instruction in the doctrines of Christianity.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Act 16:7
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
Rev 14:6
And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,
corruption_summary: Arctic island where the Norse church died out, and where Hans Egede began the Protestant mission to the Inuit in 1721 and Paul Egede printed their New Testament in 1766.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the drink trade that followed every northern mission and undid much of it. Egede's letters complain constantly of the whalers and traders who sold brandy along the coast, and the dictionary names that commerce for what it was: men from Christian nations making money by ruining the people a Christian minister had come to teach. The brandy, and then the smallpox brought in on a ship, cost more Greenlandic lives than any doctrine saved in Egede's lifetime, and an honest mission history says so.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the redirection of a servant's plan by providence. Egede went to find lost Norsemen and was not permitted to; Paul and his company “assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Act 16:7), and were sent to Macedonia instead, “assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them” (Act 16:10). The commission is broad enough to cover the change, being to “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), and the gospel is to be preached “to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6), the Inuit as truly as the Norse.

pos: n. (the North Atlantic islands reformed from Denmark, whose people had no Scripture in their own tongue until the twentieth century)
etymology: Faroese Føroyar, the sheep islands, from Old Norse fær, a sheep, and oy, an island.
biblical_def: The Faroes are the clearest case in Europe of a reformation delivered in the wrong language and left there for four hundred years. Eighteen islands of perhaps four or five thousand people under the Danish crown, they received the Reformation as Norway did, by royal ordinance in the 1530s and 1540s: the bishopric of Kirkjubour was abolished, the church lands taken, and Danish became the language of worship, Scripture, law and school. Faroese, the descendant of the Old Norse the settlers brought, went on being spoken in every house and written almost nowhere; the ballads were memorised rather than printed. The Danish church held that the islanders could follow Danish, which they could in the way a Frisian can follow Dutch, and no translation was attempted. The language was only given a standard orthography in 1846 by Venceslaus Ulricus Hammershaimb; Faroese preaching was legalised in 1903, the Gospel of Matthew appeared in 1823 and was little used, Jakup Dahl's New Testament came in 1937, and the whole Bible in Faroese only in 1961. The dictionary enters the Faroes because the Reformation's own first principle was abandoned here by the Reformation's own church, and it took four centuries to apply it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ballad as a popular song or narrative poem; orthography as the art of writing words correctly; a dialect as the form of a language peculiar to a district; and an archipelago as a sea with many islands.
webster_full: BALLAD, n. A song; originally, a solemn song of praise; now, a popular narrative song or poem.
ORTHOGRAPHY, n. The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage.
DIALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state.
ARCHIPELAGO, n. A sea interspersed with many isles; a group of islands.
TONGUE, n. The language spoken by a particular nation; speech; the power of speaking.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: North Atlantic islands reformed by Danish ordinance in the 1530s, where Danish remained the language of worship and Scripture until Faroese preaching was legalised in 1903.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Reformation forgetting its own principle, and the dictionary charges this to the Lutheran church of Denmark without qualification. The whole case against the Latin mass was that a man should hear God's word in the tongue he was born in; the Danish church preached to Faroese fishermen in Danish for three hundred and sixty years and told them it was near enough. The apostle's judgement on a tongue the hearer does not own is blunt: “I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11), and the question he asks of such speech is “how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that near enough is not the standard. Pentecost does not record that the hearers followed a related dialect with effort; each heard “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). The reading of the law at Jerusalem is the model for a public service, where they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Faroese got its New Testament in 1937 and its Bible in 1961, which is a late obedience and a real one.

pos: n. (the Arctic country of the Sami, where Thomas von Westen insisted from 1716 that the gospel be preached in their own language)
etymology: Swedish Lappland, the land of the Lapps, the older exonym for the Sami; the region spans northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
biblical_def: Lapland is the Arctic country where the question of preaching in a people's own tongue was fought out as official policy and won. The Sami, reindeer herders across the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, were nominally Christianised and substantially not: the old drums, sacred sites and noaidi practice persisted, and the Scandinavian states treated the Sami language as something to be replaced rather than used. Thomas von Westen, a Norwegian pastor appointed in 1716 to head the mission college's work in the north, took the opposite view and made it stick. He made three long journeys through the Sami districts, destroyed drums and sacred objects and was afterwards criticised for it, established some twenty schools and chapels, and founded at Trondheim the Seminarium Lapponicum to train missionaries in the Sami language, insisting against his own government that catechising, preaching and schooling be in Sami and not Danish. He died in 1727 in debt, having spent his own money on the mission. The Swedish side had the Skytteanska school and later its own Sami books. The dictionary enters Lapland because von Westen's policy was the Reformation's own principle applied at the edge of the habitable world, against a state that preferred assimilation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education; a drum as an instrument of percussion; assimilation as the act of making alike; and a herdsman as one who tends a herd.
webster_full: SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university in which young persons are instructed.
DRUM, n. A martial instrument of music, in form of a hollow cylinder, covered with vellum or head-skin.
ASSIMILATION, n. The act of bringing to a likeness, or to a conformity with something else.
HERDSMAN, n. One employed in tending herds of cattle; a manager of a herd.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Hab 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
corruption_summary: Arctic country of the Sami, where Thomas von Westen from 1716 founded schools and a seminary and required that preaching and catechising be in the Sami language.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the mission that treats a people's language as part of their heathenism. The Danish-Norwegian and Swedish states both held that the Sami should become Danes or Swedes and be taught in those languages, and von Westen spent his life and his money arguing that a Sami herdsman must hear the gospel in Sami or not hear it. The Pentecostal rule is on his side, that men heard “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), and the end of the matter is a multitude out of “all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9), not out of two Scandinavian ones.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that conversion means turning from idols to the living God, which is what the Thessalonians are commended for: “ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1Th 1:9). The dictionary holds that the Sami drums and sacred sites were idolatrous and that von Westen was right to call for their abandonment, and records that he destroyed many of them himself and was criticised for the manner of it even in his own century. The prophet's question answers the objects and not the people: “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it” (Hab 2:18).
